items.title:
Fusion dsRNA Enhances RNAi Efficiency and Broadens
the Insecticidal Spectrum
items.authors: Chen, Jiasheng; Tan, Jiayu; Chen, Yulu
items.venue: Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry
items.abstract:
Abstract 
                   RNA interference (RNAi) technology provides a precise strategy for green control of agricultural pests; however, its low efficiency and high cost still constrain its application. Constructing multitarget fusion dsRNA can significantly improve insecticidal efficiency. Using Tribolium castaneum as a model organism, three highly efficient silencing genes (RpS3, VhaSFD, and EF1) were screened. The results showed that the fusion dsRNA construct dsRVE–3 × 200 bp (200 bp per gene) had the most stable silencing performance, with an LD50 significantly lower than that of the single-gene dsRpS3. Based on the optimized parameters, a fusion dsRNA (named dsNLS) targeting Nilaparvata lugens, Locusta migratoria, and Sogatella furcifera was constructed. dsNLS was significantly superior to naked dsRNA in controlling these three pests, with mortality rates of 69.1%, 71.3%, and 93.4%, respectively, and was safe for nontarget organisms. This study confirms that fusion dsRNA can improve the insecticidal efficiency of RNAi and provides new perspectives for dsRNA design.

items.title: Keeping an Eye on Plasticity Genes: Insulin/TOR Pathway Components Mediating Nutritional Plasticity of Eyes Within and Between Sex
items.authors: Heffernan, S.;  Etchells Foisy, E.;  Saleebaan, K.;  Rajakumar, R.
items.abstract: The eyes of insects exhibit extreme morphological variation through changes in size and shape. While the model organism Drosophila melanogaster has been used to elucidate the underlying gene networks and cell-signalling pathways that regulate the patterning and growth of the eye, insight into the regulators of nutrient-dependent sizing and allometry within and between the sexes remains poorly understood. Using a screen approach of the well characterized and ancient Insulin/TOR pathway, we show that perturbations of different nodes of this pathway modulate the impact of nutritional variation on the sizing and scaling of the eye to varying degrees, and that this is further influenced by sex. When starved, wild-type flies decrease in eye size and body size proportionately in females, yet males change eye-to-body size disproportionately. Subsequently we used previously validated RNAi lines to knockdown each component of the Insulin/TOR pathway in an eye-specific manner to characterize their individual influence in modulating nutritional plasticity of eye sizing. Surprisingly, this resulted in a range of size and scaling variation, components modulating the plastic response on eye size

items.title: Identification of insecticidal double-stranded RNAs targeting the proteasome pathway in the hop flea beetle Psylliodes attenuata using dsRIP
items.authors: Cedden, D.;  Guney, G.;  Plathner, P.;  Scholten, S.;  Rostas, M.;  Kroenauer, C.
items.abstract: The hop flea beetle, Psylliodes attenuata, is a major pest of hop (Humulus lupulus), an important crop for the brewing industry. Restrictions on chemical insecticides and insecticide resistance create a need for alternative control strategies. RNA interference (RNAi) uses double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) to silence essential pest genes and cause insecticidal effects. In this study, we aimed to establish P. attenuata as an RNAi-based pest control target. We generated a transcriptome assembly using a public RNA sequencing dataset and used the dsRIP web platform to identify essential gene targets and design effective dsRNAs. Three dsRNAs targeting proteasome subunits were tested in feeding bioassays by applying them to hop leaf disks. The treatments caused significant mortality of up to 64% and feeding inhibition of up to 45%. Sequencing of small RNAs bound to the RNA-induced silencing complex identified predominantly 21-nucleotide small interfering RNAs produced from the orally delivered dsRNAs, supporting activation of the RNAi pathway. items.title: Neurofibromin Regulates Sleep Consolidation via Cholinergic Neurons in a Drosophila Model of Neurofibromatosis 1
items.authors: Atsoniou, K.;  Georganta, E.-M.;  Pfeifer, K.;  Palmer, R.;  Samiotaki, M.;  Skoulakis, E. M.
items.abstract: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) patients frequently present with fragmented, poor-quality sleep, but the neural circuits and molecular mechanisms underlying this deficit remain undefined. Using Drosophila, we show that loss of the NF1 ortholog dNf1 recapitulates the human phenotype: null mutants exhibit markedly reduced total sleep with blunted nighttime consolidation, reflected in fewer and shorter sleep bouts and elevated inter-bout activity, a recessive phenotype reproduced by independent null alleles and by pan-neuronal RNAi knockdown. Despite the broad expression of dNf1 across the adult CNS, including the mushroom bodies, ellipsoid body, dorsal fan-shaped body, and GABAergic neurons, cell-type-restricted knockdown showed the protein is dispensable for sleep regulation in each of these populations. Instead, dNf1 loss specifically in cholinergic neurons, the most abundant neuronal class in the fly brain, was sufficient to reproduce the deficient, fragmented sleep of null mutants, and restoring wild-type dNf1 to cholinergic neurons of null animals was both necessary and sufficient to rescue sleep. items.title: Development of Circadian Circuitry Underlying Feeding-Fasting Rhythms in Drosophila Larvae
items.authors: Halder, N.;  McEnaney, C.;  Hood, S. E.;  Poe, A. R.
items.abstract: Many organisms do not exhibit strong daily behavioral rhythms early in life. The consolidation of sleep and feeding to specific times of the day does not emerge until later in development. Disruptions to circadian behaviors in early life can lead to dysregulation of both neural development and metabolic homeostasis. However, the circuit mechanisms regulating feeding rhythm development are unknown. Here, we characterize the neural circuitry responsible for driving the development of feeding-fasting rhythms in early 3rd instar (L3) Drosophila larvae. We find that inactivation of both larval s-LNv circadian pacemaker neurons and SIFamide (SIFa) neurons in the pars intercerebralis disrupts feeding rhythm development. Additionally, our data indicate feeding rhythms likely emerge due to circuit connections forming between s-LNvs and SIFa neurons at the L3 stage. Finally, we show that reductions in signaling between s-LNv and SIFa neurons interfere with normal behavioral rhythm development in L3. items.authors: Gupta, Dipinte; Gnanasekaran, Prabu; Singh, Oinam Washington
items.abstract: Watermelon production is significantly affected by watermelon bud necrosis virus (WBNV), an economically important orthotospovirus in the Indian subcontinent. RNA interference (RNAi)-based approaches offer promising strategies for developing broad-spectrum antiviral resistance in susceptible plants. In this study, we evaluated the efficacy of foliar application of double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) and hairpin RNA (hpRNA) derived from the full-length NSs gene of WBNV against WBNV infection in two host plants, Nicotiana benthamiana and cowpea (Vigna unguiculata). Fluorescein-labeled dsRNA of NSs gene (dsNSs) was tracked in N. benthamiana plants, where dsNSs translocated from the treated leaf to adjacent leaves, stem, and roots. Naked dsNSs was no longer detectable in treated leaves at 5 days post-inoculation (dpi), whereas mesoporous silica nanoparticle-conjugated dsNSs (dsNSs-MSNP) remained detectable in the treated leaves beyond 5 dpi, indicating enhanced stability.
